lesson.title: Statistics: Sampling, Averages and Data
lesson.summary: Learn to interpret statistical data, compare distributions, and draw cautious conclusions using averages and spread.

objectives.text: Interpret and analyse data using statistical measures, representations, sampling and reasoned conclusions.

sections.heading: Understanding Averages and Spread
sections.body: The mean is found by adding all values and dividing by how many values there are. For 4, 5, 7, 8, 16 the mean is 40 ÷ 5 = 8, while the median is the middle value, 7. The mode is the most frequent value and the range is maximum minus minimum, here 12. The mean uses every value but is pulled by an outlier; the median is often more representative for skewed data. If every value increases by 3, the mean, median, and mode increase by 3, but the range stays the same. Compare both an average and a measure of spread before deciding whether two groups are similar. Use the same units throughout and state whether you calculated from raw data or an estimated grouped table.

sections.heading: Sampling and Representativeness
sections.body: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the smaller group measured. A random sample gives each member a known chance of selection, while a systematic sample might choose every tenth name after a random start. A convenience sample, such as asking people who happen to pass a doorway, can be biased because some groups are missed. A sample can also be too small or collected at an unrepresentative time. State the population, sampling method, and possible source of bias before interpreting a result. Even a well-designed sample provides an estimate, not certainty about every member. If a survey finds 62% of 100 sampled learners prefer option A, report the sample and avoid saying exactly 62% of all learners prefer it without further evidence.

sections.heading: Correlation and Causation
sections.body: Correlation describes how two variables change together. A positive correlation means larger values of one tend to accompany larger values of the other; a negative correlation means one tends to rise as the other falls. Correlation does not prove that one variable causes the other. Ice-cream sales and swimming incidents may both rise in summer because temperature and holidays are confounding factors. A scatter diagram can reveal strength, direction, and outliers, but it cannot by itself establish a mechanism. Distinguish an observed association from an experiment designed to test cause. Use cautious language such as ‘is associated with’ unless the evidence supports more. Also remember that no correlation does not rule out a non-linear relationship. When describing a scatter diagram, mention direction, strength, and any unusual points. A single outlier can make a weak pattern look stronger or pull an average away from the main cluster. Ask what was measured, who was included, and whether the variables were recorded under comparable conditions before drawing a conclusion.

writingActivity.title: Make a cautious statistical conclusion
writingActivity.prompt: Compare two small datasets or sampling scenarios. Calculate one average and one spread measure, then write a conclusion that names a limitation or possible source of bias.
writingActivity.wordGuide: Write 100–140 words with your calculations shown.
checklist: I chose an appropriate average and spread measure.
I described the sample or data source.
I avoided claiming causation from correlation alone.

practice.prompt: A survey of 50 students found an average height of 160cm, with a range of 10cm. Another group of 50 students had an average of 160cm, but a range of 40cm. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The first group is more consistent in height.
The second group has taller individuals on average.
Both groups have identical height distributions.
The first group contains only students of 160cm.
practice.explanation: A smaller range indicates less variation, meaning the first group is more consistent.

practice.prompt: A researcher surveys only students in a swimming club to estimate average height for all students. What is the primary statistical concern?
options: The sample size is too small.
The sample may be biased towards taller individuals.
The average height cannot be calculated.
practice.explanation: Selecting only swimmers introduces bias, as they may be taller than the general student population.

practice.prompt: Data shows that as hours spent studying increase, exam scores also increase. Which conclusion is statistically valid?
options: Studying directly causes higher exam scores.
There is a positive correlation between study time and scores.
Students who study more are naturally smarter.
Exam scores determine how much students study.
practice.explanation: The data supports a correlation, but does not prove causation or rule out other factors.
